title: The councils
hookLine: bishops met at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) to settle who Jesus is
tomorrow: the ancient churches of the east

cards: The year 325, a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Bishops arrive from across the empire, some on imperial horses paid for by the emperor Constantine.
Tradition says a few carry scars: not long before, Christians were being arrested and tortured, and some of these old men, the story goes, still limp from it.
The emperor has called them together because the church is arguing so loudly it can be heard in the marketplace.

A priest from Alexandria named Arius has been teaching that the Son of God was created, the first and greatest of all creatures, but a creature. His opponents say people are singing his ideas in catchy songs.

teach.b: A council is a gathering of church leaders to settle something together. The Greek word is synodos, a way taken together, the root of synod.

The idea goes back to the Bible: in Acts 15 the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to argue about whether new believers must keep the Jewish law, and send out a letter that says, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
At Nicaea, the bishops rejected Arius.

teach.h: NICAEA: OF ONE BEING WITH THE FATHER.
teach.b: Their statement said the Son is of one being with the Father, one Greek word, homoousios. Fifty-six years later, a second council, at Constantinople, expanded it into the creed many churches still say, the Nicene Creed.
In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer, the Son is "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made."
Then in 451, at Chalcedon, a council asked the next question: if Jesus is truly God, is he truly human too? Yes: one person, two natures, not mixed and not split.
The councils didn't invent faith in Jesus; they tried to put into words what churches were already praying and singing, and they argued fiercely doing it, with politics mixed in.
And not everyone accepted every council.
Chalcedon, especially, led to a lasting split, which is tomorrow's story. Notice how the council's creed began: not I believe, but we believe.

how: Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and others, say the Nicene Creed together at the main Sunday service, usually standing, after the readings and sermon.

games.q: you're a bishop at Nicaea. a priest says the Son of God is the greatest of creatures, but still created. what does the council say?
o: he's right: the Son is a creature.
the Son is of one being with the Father.
games.why: the council rejected Arius and said the Son is homoousios, of one being with the Father: "begotten, not made."

practice: Read the Nicene Creed once, slowly, the way you'd read a letter from someone who had suffered to write it, and notice which line stops you: the one you love, or the one you don't understand.
If you pray, say it aloud; if you don't, read it as a very old answer to a very old question.

wordCard.voice: Council. Church leaders gathered to settle a question together. From Jerusalem to Nicaea to Chalcedon.

orig.note: Greek: syn, together, and hodos, a way or road. A meeting, a council: the root of synod.

carryVoice: Your line: we believe. Much of a faith is handed on by the people who came before. See you tomorrow.
